chapters.title: urls.py
chapters.subtitle: Routing, parameters, names and reverse
chapters.summary: How a URL becomes a view call: path converters, includes, names, namespaces, and the reverse() habit that keeps links from breaking.
chapters.quick_answer: Each `path()` matches a URL pattern and calls a view. Capture values with converters such as `<int:pk>`, give every route a `name`, and build links with `{% url %}` or `reverse()` instead of writing strings by hand.

sections.title: A route is a mapping, not a regex
sections.body:
`path()` takes a route, a view and an optional name. The route is matched from the top down; the first match wins. Captured values arrive in the view as keyword arguments.

Use `re_path()` only when a path converter cannot express the pattern. Most routes do not need a regular expression.
sections.code:
from django.urls import path
from . import views

urlpatterns = [
    path("", views.home, name="home"),
    path("posts/", views.post_list, name="post-list"),
    path("posts/<int:pk>/", views.post_detail, name="post-detail"),
    path("posts/<slug:slug>/", views.post_by_slug, name="post-by-slug"),
]

sections.title: Converters decide the type
sections.body:
The converter is not decoration; it converts the string and constrains what can match.

- `str` — any non-empty string without `/`.
- `int` — digits only; the view receives an `int`.
- `slug` — letters, numbers, hyphens and underscores.
- `uuid` — a UUID object.
- `path` — like `str`, but allows `/`.

If no converter matches, Django returns 404 before your view runs.
sections.code:
path("articles/<int:year>/<slug:slug>/", views.article, name="article")

# /articles/2026/django-forms/ calls:
# views.article(request, year=2026, slug="django-forms")

sections.title: include() keeps apps self-contained
sections.body: The root URLconf should not know every route in the project. Give each app a `urls.py`, set `app_name`, and include it under a prefix. Inside templates, the namespace prevents two apps from fighting over a route called `detail`.
sections.code: # config/urls.py from django.urls import include, path urlpatterns = [ path("blog/", include("blog.urls")), path("shop/", include("shop.urls")), ] # blog/urls.py from django.urls import path from . import views app_name = "blog" urlpatterns = [ path("", views.index, name="index"), path("/", views.detail, name="detail"), ] # template {{ post.title }}

sections.title: Reverse, do not hard-code
sections.body:
Hard-coded URLs break the moment a route changes. `reverse()` builds the URL from the route name and arguments. `reverse_lazy()` is the version to use in class attributes, settings and model `get_absolute_url()` when URLs may not be loaded yet.

`{% url %}` is the template version and automatically escapes the result.
sections.note: If `reverse()` raises `NoReverseMatch`, the route name or the argument names do not match. Check the namespace first.

sections.title: Trailing slashes, 404s and custom error pages
sections.body:
Django's `CommonMiddleware` appends a trailing slash when `APPEND_SLASH=True` and the slashless URL does not match. Pick one style and stay consistent; most Django projects use trailing slashes.

A view that cannot find an object should raise `Http404` (or use `get_object_or_404`). Django then renders `404.html` at the project root when `DEBUG=False`.
sections.code:
from django.http import Http404
from django.shortcuts import get_object_or_404, render
from .models import Post

def detail(request, slug):
    post = get_object_or_404(Post, slug=slug, published=True)
    return render(request, "blog/detail.html", {"post": post})

# templates/404.html and templates/500.html are used automatically
# when DEBUG=False and the matching handler is not overridden.

pitfalls: Using `path("posts/<pk>/")` and expecting an integer; without a converter the value is a string.
Forgetting `app_name` and then using a namespace in `{% url %}`.
Hard-coding `/blog/...` in templates and breaking every link after a route rename.
Catching `ObjectDoesNotExist` and returning a 200 page for a missing object.
Putting a catch-all route above specific routes; the first match wins.
checklist: No hard-coded internal URLs in templates or views.

chapters.title: views.py
chapters.subtitle: Requests in, responses out
chapters.summary: The view is the traffic controller: read the request, call the domain logic, choose a response. Function views, class-based views, shortcuts and the errors that follow.
chapters.quick_answer: A view receives an `HttpRequest` and returns an `HttpResponse` (or raises an exception such as `Http404`). Prefer a function view until the class-based generic view genuinely removes more code than it adds.

sections.title: The contract is small
sections.body:
A view is any callable that takes a request and returns a response. The response can be HTML, JSON, a redirect, a file or an error. Django does not care how you build it.

The request gives you `method`, `GET`, `POST`, `FILES`, `headers`, `user`, `session` and `path`. The response needs a status code and content; `render()` and `JsonResponse()` handle the boilerplate.

sections.title: Function views: the honest default
sections.body:
A function view makes the flow obvious. Branch on `request.method`, validate on POST, render on GET. Keep business logic in a service or model method; the view should read like a short paragraph.

Use `require_GET` or `require_POST` to reject the wrong method explicitly instead of accidentally accepting it.
sections.note: The POST/redirect/GET pattern prevents a browser refresh from submitting the same form twice.

sections.title: The shortcuts worth knowing
sections.body:
`render()` combines a template and context. `redirect()` accepts a URL, a view name or a model with `get_absolute_url()`. `get_object_or_404()` turns a missing object into a clean 404. `get_list_or_404()` does the same for a list.

Prefer these over manual `try/except` blocks; they encode the common behaviour and are easier to read.

sections.title: Class-based views: use them when they fit
sections.body:
Generic CBVs are useful when the page is genuinely a list, a detail page or a form. They are a poor fit for a flow with several branches and custom side effects; a function view is clearer there.

Override the smallest hook: `get_queryset()` for filtering, `get_context_data()` for extra template data, `form_valid()` for a successful submit, `dispatch()` for cross-cutting checks. Call `super()` unless you intentionally replace the behaviour.
sections.code:
from django.contrib.auth.mixins import LoginRequiredMixin
from django.views.generic import ListView

from .models import Post

class PostList(LoginRequiredMixin, ListView):
    model = Post
    template_name = "blog/post_list.html"
    context_object_name = "posts"
    paginate_by = 20

    def get_queryset(self):
        return (
            super()
            .get_queryset()
            .filter(author=self.request.user)
            .select_related("author")
        )

    def get_context_data(self, **kwargs):
        context = super().get_context_data(**kwargs)
        context["draft_count"] = self.get_queryset().filter(status="draft").count()
        return context
sections.note: For a FormView, `form_valid()` usually saves and then returns `super().form_valid(form)` so the configured `success_url` redirect happens.

sections.title: Pagination without loading the whole table
sections.body:
`ListView` paginates with `paginate_by`. The template receives `page_obj` and `paginator`; `page_obj.object_list` holds the current page and `page_obj.has_next` drives the next link. The `?page=` parameter is handled for you.

For a function view, use `Paginator` directly. Always order the queryset; an unordered paginated query can return the same row twice across pages. Keep the page size bounded so a client cannot ask for 10,000 rows.
sections.note: An unordered queryset can produce unstable pages. Add `order_by()` before paginating.

sections.title: Errors and status codes
sections.body:
Raise `Http404` when the resource does not exist. Return `HttpResponseBadRequest` for malformed input, `HttpResponseForbidden` for a permission failure, and `HttpResponseNotAllowed` for the wrong method. Do not return a 200 page that silently says “not found”; clients, caches and tests all rely on the status code.

For expected form errors, re-render the form with a 200 status and field-level messages. For an unhandled exception, let Django return 500 and log it.

pitfalls: Doing complex business logic in the view instead of a service or model method.
Forgetting to return a response on one branch and getting `ValueError: The view didn't return an HttpResponse object`.
Using `request.GET["q"]` without a default; a missing parameter raises `KeyError`.
Trusting `request.POST` for a value without validating it through a form.
Overriding `dispatch()` without calling `super()` and silently skipping the view.
checklist: Every branch returns a response or raises an exception.
POST handling uses a form and redirects on success.
Missing objects produce a 404, not a 200 with an empty page.
Permissions are checked before side effects.
The view reads like a short paragraph, not a second models.py.

chapters.title: Templates
chapters.subtitle: Inheritance, tags, filters and escaping
chapters.summary: The Django template language without the cargo cult: inheritance, context lookup, the tags you actually need, and why autoescaping is not optional.
chapters.quick_answer: Put a `base.html` with named blocks at the project level, extend it in each app template, and keep logic out of the template. Use `{{ value }}` for output, `{% tag %}` for control, and never disable autoescaping for user data.

sections.title: Inheritance in one picture
sections.body:
A child template extends a base and fills blocks. The base owns the document shell, navigation and footer; the child owns one screen. `{{ block.super }}` keeps the parent content when you only want to add to it.

Use `{% include %}` for a fragment reused inside a page, and `{% extends %}` for a page that fills a layout.
sections.code:
{% block content %}{% endblock %}
{% extends "base.html" %} {% block title %}Posts · {{ block.super }}{% endblock %} {% block content %}

{{ page_title }}

{% include "blog/_post_list.html" with posts=object_list only %} {% endblock %}
sections.note: `only` prevents the included template from seeing the parent context; it makes the fragment's dependencies explicit.

sections.title: Variables use dot lookup, not Python
sections.body:
`{{ post.author.name }}` tries, in order: dictionary key, attribute, list index. You cannot call a function with arguments, do arithmetic, or use arbitrary Python. That is a feature: templates stay presentation-only.

Missing values render as an empty string by default. Use `default`, `default_if_none` and `{% if %}` to make empty states explicit.

sections.title: The tags you will use daily
sections.body:
Tags control flow and URL generation. `{% url %}` reverses a named route; `{% static %}` builds a static URL; `{% csrf_token %}` adds the hidden CSRF field to every POST form. `{% for %}` has an `{% empty %}` branch that is easy to forget.

`{% with %}` and `{% cycle %}` are occasionally useful. Avoid custom template tags until a real repetition proves the need.

sections.title: Rendering a form without guessing
sections.body:
`{{ form.as_p }}` is fine for a prototype. For real layout, render fields explicitly: label, widget, errors and help text are separate pieces. Always render `form.non_field_errors` and add `{% csrf_token %}` inside the form.

If you render the `<input>` yourself, keep `{{ field.id_for_label }}` and `{{ field.html_name }}` so labels and POST data still work.
sections.code:
{% csrf_token %} {{ form.non_field_errors }}
{{ field.label_tag }} {{ field }} {% for error in field.errors %}

{{ error }}

{% endfor %} {% if field.help_text %}

{{ field.help_text }}

{% endif %}

sections.title: Autoescaping is the safety net
sections.body:
By default, `{{ value }}` escapes `<`, `>`, `&`, quotes and apostrophes. That is why a comment containing `<script>` renders as text instead of executing.

`|safe` and `{% autoescape off %}` turn the net off. Use them only for HTML you generated yourself and trust. If you need to mark a fragment as safe, prefer a small template include or a sanitising library over a blanket `|safe`.
sections.note: A Content Security Policy is a second line of defence, not a replacement for escaping.

sections.title: Static files and URLs
sections.body:
`{% static %}` builds a URL from `STATIC_URL`. During development, `runserver` serves static files when `django.contrib.staticfiles` is installed. In production, `collectstatic` copies them to `STATIC_ROOT` and a web server (or WhiteNoise) serves them.

Never hard-code `/static/...`; the storage backend may add a manifest hash or a CDN prefix.
sections.code:
{% load static %}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="{% static 'css/site.css' %}">
<script src="{% static 'js/app.js' %}" defer></script>

<!-- cache-busting is handled by the storage backend -->

pitfalls: Putting business logic in templates; it is hard to test and impossible to reuse.
Forgetting `{% csrf_token %}` and getting a 403 on every POST.
Using `|safe` on user input and creating an XSS hole.
Assuming `{% extends %}` can appear anywhere except the first tag in the file.
Loading static files with a hard-coded path that breaks under a manifest storage backend.
checklist: Base template has named blocks and a content block.
User data is escaped; `|safe` is reviewed.
Empty states handled with `{% empty %}` or `{% if %}`.
